sources.name: THC Cannabis Encyclopedia Volume 13 — Terpenes, Volatiles, and Other Secondary Metabolites
sources.notes: Controls THC explanations, interpretation guardrails, cannabis-specific teaching language, and claims discipline.

sources.name: PubChem
sources.notes: Primary normalization source for CIDs, names, formulae, molecular weights, InChIKeys, SMILES, synonyms, and structure identifiers.

sources.name: COCONUT natural products database
sources.notes: Primary bulk natural-products feed for the global terpene/terpenoid registry. September 2026 CSV-lite release is versioned and ingested as source candidates; preserve upstream IDs/release and do not auto-promote candidates to reviewed THC records.

sources.name: Peer-reviewed cannabis chemistry and terpene-synthase literature
sources.notes: Stores sample context, analytical method, compound occurrence, TPS evidence, and study-level provenance.

sources.name: Qualified cannabis laboratory and published sample datasets
sources.notes: Never collapse source samples into a single permanent strain percentage. Preserve lab, date, units, method, and provenance.

sources.name: DTF Genetics breeding, phenotype, pedigree, and future COA records
sources.notes: Connect parent chemistry to measured offspring and selections. Predictions remain probabilistic until supported by offspring data.

sources.name: The phytochemical diversity of commercial Cannabis in the United States — published dataset
sources.notes: Published cleaned laboratory dataset spanning multiple U.S. testing labs. Preserve sample-level records and dataset-normalized strain_slug; do not turn cultivar labels into fixed chemistry values.

sources.name: Booth JK, Page JE, Bohlmann J. Terpene synthases from Cannabis sativa.
sources.notes: Primary functional characterization source for multiple Cannabis sativa terpene synthases. Table 2 and Fig. 4 are key gene-product evidence locations.

sources.name: Booth JK et al. Terpene Synthases and Terpene Variation in Cannabis sativa.
sources.notes: Expanded terpene synthase family and terpene variation reference for future gene/cultivar evidence.

sources.name: LOTUS Initiative / Natural Products Online
sources.notes: Secondary open natural-products occurrence source intended for cross-checking organism/occurrence evidence and expanding provenance. Do not merge identities by common name; use exact structure identifiers.

sources.name: Bueno J et al. The preservation and augmentation of volatile terpenes in cannabis inflorescence.
sources.notes: Cannabis inflorescence storage/packaging study using HS GC-MS. Preserve study-specific storage conditions and conflict-of-interest context.

sources.name: Kim YW et al. Safety evaluation and risk assessment of d-Limonene.
sources.notes: Toxicology/risk review for d-limonene. Use only for the exposure routes and endpoints discussed by the source; do not generalize to cannabis inhalation.

sources.name: Sköld M et al. Contact allergens formed on air exposure of linalool.
sources.notes: Experimental autoxidation and sensitization work on linalool and oxidation products; includes chromatographic/NMR identification and LLNA testing.

sources.name: Api AM et al. RIFM fragrance ingredient safety assessment, β-caryophyllene.
sources.notes: Fragrance-use safety assessment covering genotoxicity, repeated dose, reproductive, respiratory, phototoxicity/photoallergenicity, sensitization, and environmental endpoints.

sources.name: Surendran S et al. Myrcene—What Are the Potential Health Benefits of This Flavouring and Aroma Agent?
sources.notes: Review of β-myrcene occurrence, biological research, and toxicological profile; explicitly notes limited human evidence for proposed biological effects.

sources.name: Botvid S et al. Ten Years of Patch Testing to Hydroperoxides of Limonene and Linalool.
sources.notes: Human patch-testing dataset focused on hydroperoxides formed by autoxidation of limonene and linalool. Applies to contact-allergy context, not general cannabis exposure.

sources.name: National Toxicology Program. Toxicology and Carcinogenesis Studies of α-Pinene Administered by Inhalation.
sources.notes: 2026 NTP chronic and subchronic inhalation toxicology/carcinogenicity report in rats and mice. Animal hazard evidence only; exposure concentrations and species must remain explicit and must not be converted into a human cannabis-use risk estimate.

sources.name: Menezes IO et al. Biological properties of terpinolene evidenced by in silico, in vitro and in vivo studies: A systematic review.
sources.notes: Systematic review of terpinolene biological studies. Explicitly notes poor characterization of in-vivo efficacy and safety and limited preclinical/clinical depth.

sources.name: Wei Q et al. Toxicity study of the volatile constituents of Myoga utilizing acute dermal irritation assays and the Guinea-pig Maximization test.
sources.notes: Dermal irritation/sensitization study of myoga volatiles including α-pinene and β-pinene. Route- and concentration-specific animal evidence; not an inhalation or typical cannabis exposure study.

sources.name: Borges AS et al. Assessment of the Acute Toxicity and Anxiolytic-Like Effect of α-Humulene in Adult Zebrafish.
sources.notes: Acute intraperitoneal zebrafish toxicity/behavior study. Animal model and injection route must remain explicit; not evidence of human safety or inhaled cannabis effects.

sources.name: PubChem PUG-View experimental property records
sources.notes: Caches source-preserved PubChem PUG-View reports for experimental physical properties, sensory evidence, and natural occurrence text. Do not collapse multiple reports into one universal value; do not reinterpret boiling point as a vaping recommendation; do not treat a lower odor threshold as proof of greater cannabis importance or psychoactive effect; do not convert reported natural occurrence into quantified abundance or Cannabis occurrence without separate evidence.

sources.name: Morello V et al. Light Quality Impacts Vertical Growth Rate, Phytochemical Yield and Cannabinoid Production Efficiency in Cannabis sativa.
sources.notes: Controlled light-spectrum experiment in Babbas Erkle Cookies with terpene quantification. Treatment effects are chemotype/experiment-specific and must not be generalized as universal lighting recipes.

sources.name: Reichel P et al. Impacts of Different Light Spectra on CBD, CBDA and Terpene Concentrations in Relation to the Flower Positions of Different Cannabis Sativa L. Strains.
sources.notes: Three-strain greenhouse experiment showing terpene interactions among spectrum, strain, and flower position. Preserve genotype and position dependence.

sources.name: Holweg MMSF et al. The role of red and white light in optimizing growth and accumulation of plant specialized metabolites at two light intensities in medical cannabis.
sources.notes: Medical cannabis light-spectrum and PPFD experiment. Total terpenoid effects were treatment-specific; do not convert to universal cultivation advice.

sources.name: Birenboim M et al. In Pursuit of Optimal Quality: Cultivar-Specific Drying Approaches for Medicinal Cannabis.
sources.notes: Controlled-atmosphere versus traditional drying study in two medicinal cannabis chemovars. Preserve cultivar and drying-condition specificity.

sources.name: Goffman FD et al. Impact of Electron Beam Treatment and Storage Duration on Microbial Load and Chemical Stability of Dried Hemp Flowers.
sources.notes: 2025 two-cultivar dried-hemp study comparing electron-beam irradiation and 12-week storage. Individual terpene and class-level changes are treatment-, cultivar-, and time-specific and must not be generalized into universal storage rates.

sources.name: Gertsch J et al. Beta-caryophyllene is a dietary cannabinoid.
sources.notes: Primary mechanistic study reporting selective CB2 binding/function for (E)-β-caryophyllene, plus downstream signaling assays. Mechanistic evidence is not a clinical efficacy claim.

sources.name: Pei S et al. Exploring the physiological response differences of β-caryophyllene, linalool and citral inhalation and their anxiolytic potential.
sources.notes: 48-person controlled odor-inhalation experiment with four randomized groups and stress-task measures. Small group size and short exposure window must remain explicit; do not convert into broad therapeutic claims.

sources.name: Lorenzetti BB et al. Myrcene mimics the peripheral analgesic activity of lemongrass tea.
sources.notes: Rat and mouse nociception/hyperalgesia models using myrcene. Animal pharmacology only; not direct evidence of analgesic efficacy in humans or cannabis products.

sources.name: Heuberger E et al. Effects of chiral fragrances on human autonomic nervous system parameters and self-evaluation.
sources.notes: Controlled fragrance-inhalation experiment in 20 healthy volunteers comparing limonene/carvone enantiomers. Supports enantiomer- and odor-context-specific human responses, not general cannabis effects.

sources.name: Falk-Filipsson A et al. d-Limonene exposure to humans by inhalation: uptake, distribution, elimination, and effects on pulmonary function.
sources.notes: Controlled human exposure-chamber study of d-limonene toxicokinetics and pulmonary endpoints at three concentrations. Occupational-style exposure context; not typical cannabis-use exposure.

sources.name: Wojtunik-Kulesza KA. Toxicity of Selected Monoterpenes and Essential Oils Rich in These Compounds.
sources.notes: Review includes α-terpinene among selected monoterpenes with toxicological literature. Preserve dose/context dependence and do not generalize review findings to cannabis exposure.

sources.name: Alves et al. Toxicogenetic profile and antioxidant evaluation of gamma-terpinene: Molecular docking and in vitro and in vivo assays.
sources.notes: Mixed in silico, in vitro, plant-cell, invertebrate, and rat toxicogenetic study. Model-specific findings must remain explicit.

sources.name: Cho S et al. High-dose squalene ingestion increases type I procollagen and decreases ultraviolet-induced DNA damage in human skin in vivo but is associated with transient adverse effects.
sources.notes: Human high-dose oral supplementation study in older women. Applies only to the tested oral doses and duration; not evidence about inhalation or cannabis exposure.

sources.name: EFSA NDA Panel. Scientific opinion on the tolerable upper intake level for preformed vitamin A and β-carotene.
sources.notes: Authoritative dietary/supplement risk assessment. Background dietary β-carotene and supplemental β-carotene are treated separately; not a cannabis exposure assessment.

sources.name: Api AM et al. RIFM fragrance ingredient safety assessment, 3,7-dimethyl-1,3,6-octatriene, CAS 13877-91-3.
sources.notes: Safety assessment is registered against CAS 13877-91-3 / 3,7-dimethyl-1,3,6-octatriene and is not treated here as E/Z-isomer-resolved evidence.

sources.name: Ibrahim EA et al. Analysis of Terpenes in Cannabis sativa L. Using GC/MS: Method Development, Validation, and Application.
sources.notes: Validated GC-MS method for selected cannabis terpenes using ethyl-acetate extraction, n-tridecane internal standard, reference standards, and AOAC-oriented validation.

sources.name: Micalizzi G et al. Cannabis Sativa L.: a comprehensive review on the analytical methodologies for cannabinoids and terpenes characterization.
sources.notes: Review of extraction, GC, HPLC, and GC×GC approaches for cannabinoid and terpene characterization in cannabis matrices.

sources.name: Farré-Armengol G et al. β-Ocimene, a Key Floral and Foliar Volatile Involved in Multiple Interactions between Plants and Other Organisms.
sources.notes: Plant-ecology review covering floral emission, pollinator context, herbivory-induced emissions, and tritrophic interactions. Keep E/Z identity scope explicit.

sources.name: Shalu S et al. Microbial Squalene: A Sustainable Alternative for the Cosmetics and Pharmaceutical Industry - A Review.
sources.notes: Review of squalene production, metabolic engineering, and cosmetic/pharmaceutical applications with emphasis on sustainable non-shark sources.

sources.name: Kläui H, Bauernfeind JC. Carotenoids as food colorants.
sources.notes: Review of commercial carotenoid synthesis and food-colorant applications including β-carotene.

sources.name: Kim DS et al. Alpha-Pinene Exhibits Anti-Inflammatory Activity Through the Suppression of MAPKs and the NF-κB Pathway in Mouse Peritoneal Macrophages.
sources.notes: LPS-stimulated mouse peritoneal macrophage study. In-vitro/mechanistic evidence only; not a human therapeutic outcome.

sources.name: Phillips CA et al. Identification and Quantification of the Antimicrobial Components of a Citrus Essential Oil Vapor.
sources.notes: In-vitro antimicrobial vapor study testing β-pinene separately and in mixtures. Does not establish clinical antimicrobial efficacy or cannabis inhalation effects.

sources.name: Pereira-de-Morais L et al. Myorelaxant action of Dysphania ambrosioides essential oil and its major constituent α-terpinene in isolated rat trachea.
sources.notes: Ex-vivo isolated rat tracheal smooth-muscle study. Mechanistic organ-bath evidence only; not a human respiratory treatment claim.

sources.name: Lou-Bonafonte JM et al. Current Insights into the Biological Action of Squalene.
sources.notes: Systematic review spanning in-vitro, animal, and human/bioavailability evidence. Review summaries must not be converted into a universal therapeutic claim.

sources.name: Tang G et al. Short-term and long-term conversion of beta-carotene to retinol in adults as assessed by a stable-isotope reference method.
sources.notes: Human stable-isotope feeding study of β-carotene conversion to retinol. Metabolic conversion evidence, not a general supplement-benefit claim.
